title: Diet Pattern Explorer
description: Interactive simulation of 200 simulated people with diet quality and low-mood scores. Learners set the true effect of diet on mood and switch hidden factors (food access, sleep, and earlier low mood that changes eating) on and off, then compare an observational study, which shows a correlation created by confounding and reverse causation, with a randomized trial, in which a coin flip balances the hidden factors.
creator: Aaryav Sharma
subject: neuroscience (gut-brain axis)
publisher: Gut Check: The Neuroscience of How Your Gut and Brain Talk
learningObjectives: Distinguish association from causation in nutrition research.
Explain how confounders and reverse causation can create a diet-mood correlation even when diet has no true effect.
Explain why random assignment in a trial balances hidden factors, and why small trials still vary by chance.
prerequisites: Reading a scatter plot and the idea of a correlation
The difference between correlation and cause
keyQuestions: Can diet and mood be linked even if diet has no effect on mood?
Which hidden factors create the strongest misleading link?
Why does a coin flip remove confounding?
Why do results from small trials change from sample to sample?
misconceptions: A strong correlation in a big observational study proves cause.
Researchers can always measure and adjust for every hidden factor.
A randomized trial always gives the exact true answer, no matter how small.
If diet and mood are linked, changing diet must change mood.
